column1: Could you help me, please?|helping,lifting|Could you help me, please?~Of course. What do you need?~This box is too heavy for me.~I can hold the other end.|Ask for help with one specific task, rather than only saying Help.|Could you help me carry this box, please?|Make the request specific so the listener knows what help is needed. Please adds politeness but does not replace a clear request.

Could you explain that again?|listening,whiteboard|Could you explain that again?~Certainly. Which part was unclear?~Where we meet after the walk.~At the cafe beside the station, at four.|Ask for another explanation and identify the exact point you missed.|Could you explain the meeting place again? I missed where we go after the walk.|A focused follow-up is more helpful than pretending to understand or asking the speaker to repeat everything.

Let me check that I understand.|document,strategy|Let me check that I understand.~Go ahead.~We book the room now, but confirm the guest list on Friday?~Exactly. The room booking does not depend on the final number.|Check an arrangement in which the room is booked today and the guest list is confirmed on Friday.|Let me check that I understand. We book the room today and confirm the guest list on Friday, correct?|Follow the phrase with your own paraphrase, then leave room for correction. It is a check, not a declaration that your account is final.

Would you mind if we considered another option?|discussion,map|The first venue is cheap, but the stairs may be difficult for some guests.~Would you mind if we considered another option?~Not at all. What do you suggest?~The library room has level access and is near the bus stop.|Suggest an alternative venue politely and give one concrete reason for considering it.|Would you mind if we considered the library room? It has level access.|Would you mind if we + past form can make a tentative suggestion: considered. Not at all commonly grants the request.

I see your point, although I would qualify it slightly.|discussion,listening|A successful event should be exciting from beginning to end.~I see your point, although I would qualify it slightly. Guests also need somewhere quiet.~Would that spoil the atmosphere?~Not if it is separate from the main activity.|A colleague says every part of an event must be intense. Agree with the useful part and add one clear limitation.|I see your point, although I would qualify it slightly. The main activity can be lively, but a quiet area would give guests a choice.|Qualify means limit or refine a claim here. State the actual reservation rather than leaving the phrase unsupported.

I would distinguish between the intention and its consequences.|document,discussion|The rule was introduced to make registration fair.~I would distinguish between the intention and its consequences.~You think it affected people differently?~Yes. Requiring a phone excluded some of the people it was meant to help.|A well-meant phone-only booking rule excludes people without phones. Separate the aim from the result in your response.|The intention was fair access, but one consequence was excluding people without phones.|This distinction acknowledges an aim without treating a good aim as proof of a good outcome. Name both elements concretely.

Let’s make lunch together.|meal,sharing|Let's make lunch together.~Good idea. What can I do?~You can wash the vegetables.~And you can make the soup.|Invite someone to make lunch and give them one clear task.|Let's make lunch together. Could you wash the vegetables?|Let's suggests doing something together. It is different from telling the other person to do the whole task.

I can bring fruit if you bring bread.|sharing,produce|I can bring fruit if you bring bread.~That works. How many people are coming?~Four.~Then I will bring enough bread for four.|Agree on contributions to a picnic for four people using if.|I can bring fruit if you bring enough bread for four people.|The if-clause makes the arrangement conditional. Confirm the other person agrees rather than treating the offer as an assignment.

Could we agree on who will do each task?|checklist,strategy|Everyone has offered to help, but no jobs are assigned.~Could we agree on who will do each task?~I will handle registration. Could you prepare the tables?~Yes. Who will lock up afterward?|A group has volunteers but no assigned closing task. Ask a question that makes responsibility clear.|Could we agree on who will lock up after the event?|Clarify responsibility, timing and any handover. Saying everyone will help can leave essential tasks unowned.

What would make this plan workable for everyone?|strategy,listening|The afternoon slot works for most people.~What would make this plan workable for everyone?~One volunteer cannot arrive before three.~We could give her the later shift and confirm cover for the opening.|A volunteer cannot arrive before three. Propose a change that preserves coverage without dismissing the constraint.|Assign her the later shift and arrange cover for the opening.|Workable means possible to carry out in practice. Invite constraints and specific adjustments, not merely a general vote of approval.

Before we optimise the process, let’s clarify its purpose.|whiteboard,notebook|The new form would make registration two minutes faster.~Before we optimise the process, let's clarify its purpose.~Do you mean speed may not be the main objective?~Yes. Clear access for people unfamiliar with the system matters too.|A team measures only registration speed. State another relevant purpose and how it could change the design.|If the purpose includes access for newcomers, the form may need clearer guidance even if it takes slightly longer.|Optimise is British spelling; optimize is American spelling. A faster process is not automatically better if it loses its purpose.

Agreement is meaningful only when dissent remains possible.|discussion,whiteboard|Everyone approved the plan in the meeting.~Could anyone object without risking their place in the group?~I am not sure.~Agreement is meaningful only when dissent remains possible.|Explain why unanimous approval may not establish genuine consent if people fear consequences for objecting.|People may comply because dissent feels unsafe, so apparent agreement may not express their actual judgment.|Dissent means expressing disagreement. The statement concerns conditions for meaningful agreement, not a requirement that someone must always object.

I have time for one small thing.|tea,book|Do you want to start a big job before breakfast?~I have time for one small thing.~What will you do?~Read one page and then leave.|Choose one small activity that fits a ten-minute gap.|I can read a page or make a cup of tea.|One small thing limits the commitment. Choose a task that genuinely fits rather than naming several tasks as one.

I am trying to do one thing at a time.|phone,notebook|You have put your phone away.~I am trying to do one thing at a time.~Are you finishing the letter first?~Yes. I will check messages afterward.|A friend interrupts your letter with a non-urgent message. Explain when you will respond.|I am trying to do one thing at a time. I will reply after I finish the letter.|The present continuous describes a current effort. Trying does not claim the habit is already perfect.

I would rather make a small change that I can keep.|calendar,morning|Are you going to study for two hours every morning?~I would rather make a small change that I can keep.~What seems manageable?~Ten minutes after breakfast, at least to begin with.|Replace an unrealistic two-hour daily promise with a sustainable alternative using would rather.|I would rather read for ten minutes after breakfast and keep doing it.|Would rather + base verb expresses a preference. Do not add to before the verb: would rather make.

I want my schedule to reflect what matters to me.|calendar,walk|Your calendar is full, but you sound dissatisfied.~I want my schedule to reflect what matters to me.~What is missing?~Time with my sister. I keep treating it as optional.|Name one calendar change that makes a stated priority visible in practice.|Reserve a regular time to see the person you say matters to you.|Reflect means show or express here. Link the value to an actual allocation of time rather than only an aspiration.

The aim is to make the valued choice easier to repeat.|book,minimal|Why leave the book beside the kettle?~The aim is to make the valued choice easier to repeat.~So you are changing the setting rather than demanding more willpower?~Exactly. The cue helps me begin reading while the water heats.|Suggest one environmental change that makes a valued reading habit easier to repeat.|Leave a book where the routine already pauses, such as beside the kettle.|Valued means regarded as worthwhile. Making a choice easier should support agency, not remove the ability to choose otherwise.

A life cannot be judged solely by the efficiency of its arrangements.|relaxing,calendar|The revised routine saves forty minutes a day.~Does that tell us whether the day is better?~Not by itself.~A life cannot be judged solely by the efficiency of its arrangements.|A routine saves time but removes valued conversations. Explain why efficiency alone cannot settle its merit.|The saved time is one benefit, but losing meaningful relationships or experiences may outweigh it.|Solely limits the claim: efficiency is relevant but insufficient. The phrase does not say efficiency has no value.

Present simple|morning,tea|Does Mia make breakfast every day?~She makes it on weekdays.~And at weekends?~We make it together.|Correct the subject-verb agreement: She make breakfast, but we makes lunch.|She makes breakfast, but we make lunch.|Use the base verb after I, you, we and they. In affirmative clauses, add -s or -es after he, she and it.

Going to for plans|calendar,itinerary|What are you going to do on Saturday?~I am going to visit the museum.~Is your brother coming?~Yes. We are going to meet at the entrance.|Your friend has already decided to visit the museum. Complete: She ___ going to visit it. We ___ going to meet her.|She is going to visit it. We are going to meet her.|Use am, is or are + going to + base verb for an intended action. Match be to the subject; do not change the main verb.

First conditional|rain,map|Will we still walk if it rains?~If it rains, we will use the covered route.~What if that is closed?~We will check before leaving.|Correct the conditional: If it will rain, we will take the bus.|If it rains, we will take the bus.|For this future condition use if + present simple, then will + base verb. Do not normally put will in the if-clause.

Although and despite|rain,station|Was the train delay enough to cancel the visit?~Although we arrived late, we still saw the exhibition.~Did you have to hurry?~Yes, but despite the delay, the visit was worthwhile.|Rewrite Although the train was late, we enjoyed the visit using despite.|Despite the late train, we enjoyed the visit.|Although introduces a clause with a subject and verb; despite takes a noun phrase or an -ing form. Avoid despite of.

Inversion after only then|document,halloween-costume|Did you notice the missing condition at once?~No. I read the second page first.~And after that?~Only then did I realize that advance registration was required.|Rewrite We read the second page. At that moment we understood the deadline as a sentence beginning Only then.|Only then did we understand the deadline.|After fronted Only then use auxiliary + subject + main verb. Past simple uses did + base verb: did we understand, not understood.

Concessive fronting|calendar,document|Was the plan useful?~Useful as it was, it could not anticipate every guest's preference.~Would you abandon it?~No. I would leave room to adjust it.|Rewrite Although the plan was useful, it had limits using adjective + as.|Useful as the plan was, it had limits.|Adjective + as + subject + verb concedes a point in a formal style. Do not add although to the same construction.

We + verb|meal,sharing|Who makes lunch?~We make it together.~What do you do first?~We wash the vegetables.|Correct: We washes the vegetables and makes soup.|We wash the vegetables and make soup.|After we use the base form in an affirmative present-simple clause. Do not add the third-person singular -s.

Be going to + verb|itinerary,map|Have you decided where to meet?~We are going to meet near the lake.~Are you going to bring lunch?~Yes. I have already bought the food.|Correct: We going to meet by the lake.|We are going to meet by the lake.|Be is required: am/is/are going to + base verb. This pattern often reports an intention already formed.

If + present, will + verb|community,checklist|Can we finish before lunch?~If we share the work, we will finish in time.~Then I can prepare the tables.~And I will organize the materials.|Combine these ideas in a first conditional: We share the work. We finish before lunch.|If we share the work, we will finish before lunch.|Use present simple in the if-clause and will + base verb in the result clause for this possible future outcome.

If we had…, we could…|room,chair|Could we include another display?~If we had a larger room, we could.~But the current room is already full.~Then we should not promise the extra display.|You do not have a larger room. Rewrite A larger room would let us add seating using If we had.|If we had a larger room, we could add seating.|If + past simple can present an unreal or hypothetical current situation; could expresses a possible result, not a guarantee.

Although / despite|rain,document|Did the time limit prevent testing?~Although time was limited, we tested the plan.~So the main checks were completed?~Yes, despite the short session.|Choose the grammatical option and explain: Although the short session / Despite the short session, we completed the checks.|Despite the short session is grammatical because it is followed by a noun phrase.|Although + clause; despite + noun phrase or -ing form. A different structure is needed after each connector.

Not until… did…|document,strategy|When did the disagreement become clearer?~Not until we stated our assumptions did we understand it.~So the facts had not changed?~No. What changed was our understanding of the starting points.|Correct: Not until we explained the rules we did understand the problem.|Not until we explained the rules did we understand the problem.|Invert the auxiliary and subject in the main clause, not inside the not until clause: Not until we explained ... did we understand.

At + a time|clock,alarm|What time do you wake up?~At seven.~Do we meet at eight?~Yes, by the station.|Choose the right preposition: We meet ___ eight o'clock.|at|Use at with clock times. Compare on Monday and in October; these expressions take different prepositions.

Adverbs of frequency|morning,book|Do you read before work every day?~I usually do, but not on Fridays.~Are you often in a hurry then?~Yes. That is my early shift.|Put often in the usual position: I am tired after work. I read on the train.|I am often tired after work. I often read on the train.|Frequency adverbs usually go before a main verb but after be: often read; am often tired.

Used to + verb|phone,morning|Do you still check messages during breakfast?~I used to, but now I leave the phone in another room.~Was it difficult to change?~At first. I kept reaching for it.|Correct the negative past-habit sentence: I did not used to read before work.|I did not use to read before work.|Used to + base verb describes a past habit or state no longer true. After did or did not, use use to.

Present perfect continuous|plant,notebook|How long have you been keeping these garden notes?~I have been recording the changes since March.~Every day?~Most days, especially when new leaves appear.|Complete with since or for: I have been recording changes ___ March and ___ several months.|since March; for several months|Have/has been + -ing can describe an activity continuing to now. Since introduces a starting point; for introduces a duration.

What-cleft sentences|minimal,calendar|Did the new planner solve the problem?~What I needed was more space between appointments.~Not a more detailed timetable?~Exactly. I was solving the wrong problem.|Emphasize the needed thing with a what-cleft: I needed a quiet place, not another app.|What I needed was a quiet place, not another app.|A what-clause plus be focuses attention on particular information: What I needed was X. Keep the tense appropriate to the context.

Were it not for…|sharing,discussion|Would you keep attending without the informal conversations?~Were it not for those conversations, the sessions would feel rather empty.~Then the unplanned part matters?~More than the official timetable suggests.|Rewrite If it were not for the volunteers, the event would be impossible using inversion.|Were it not for the volunteers, the event would be impossible.|Formal inversion of If it were not for; omit if. It imagines the absence of a present condition, not a completed past event.
